data, their verification and quality control, the dataset with the exposure
variables for 2009-2020, and the municipal maps and time series of single and
compound exposure.

The tables and the figures of this page can be downloaded: each table has an

# Methodology {#sec-methodology}

```{r}
#| label: setup-methodology
#| include: false
source(here::here("Code", "00_setup.R"))
source(here::here("Code", "01_functions.R"))
source(here::here("Code", "02_plot_style.R"))
library(knitr)
theme_set(theme_report())
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")
fmt <- function(x, digits = 0) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")

# Every number quoted in the methodology is computed here, from the
# configuration, the inputs and the outputs of the scripts
method <- list()
method$municipalities <- study_municipalities()
method$years <- get_param("study", "years")
method$lags <- unlist(get_param("design", "lags_days"))
method$lag_buffer <- max(method$lags)
method$reference_years <- get_param("temperature", "percentile_reference_years")
method$percentiles <- unlist(get_param("temperature", "percentile_thresholds"))
method$durations <- unlist(get_param("temperature", "min_consecutive_days"))
method$absolute_c <- get_param("temperature", "absolute_threshold_celsius")
method$ehf_percentile <- get_param("temperature", "ehf_reference_percentile")
method$ehf_days <- get_param("temperature", "ehf_acclimatisation_days")
method$heatwave_main <- get_param("models", "heatwave_main")
method$ozone_main <- paste0(get_param("air_pollution", "ozone_series_main"), "_",
                            get_param("air_pollution", "interpolation_method_main"))
method$cutoff_main <- get_param("models", "ozone_cutoff_main")
method$cutoffs <- unlist(get_param("air_pollution", "ozone_percentile_cutoffs"))
method$interpolation <- get_param("interpolation")
method$station_rules <- get_param("station_series")
method$stations <- fread(here::here(method$station_rules$stations_file), encoding = "UTF-8")
# Period asked for in the download of the hourly records, as written in the file names
method$hourly_period <- regmatches(method$station_rules$hourly_file_pattern,
                                   gregexpr("[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}",
                                            method$station_rules$hourly_file_pattern))[[1]]
stopifnot(length(method$hourly_period) == 2)
# Months of the reanalysis that the scripts read (month names written in
# English here: date formats follow the language of the computer)
method$cams_months <- sub(".*_([0-9]{6})_.*", "\\1", cams_month_files())
month_year <- function(yyyymm) paste(month.name[as.integer(substr(yyyymm, 5, 6))], substr(yyyymm, 1, 4))

# The exposure dataset and its days of analysis
method_exposure <- fread(derived_path("exposure_2009_2020.csv"), encoding = "UTF-8")
method_exposure[, date := as.Date(date)]
method_days <- method_exposure[in_study_period == TRUE & warm_season == TRUE]
method$rows <- nrow(method_exposure)
method$days <- uniqueN(method_days$date)
method$municipality_days <- nrow(method_days)
method$heatwave_columns <- grep("^hw_", names(method_exposure), value = TRUE)
method$ozone_flags <- grep("_gt_p[0-9]+$", names(method_exposure), value = TRUE)
method$share_hot_study <- 100 * mean(method_days$hot_p95)
method$share_heatwave_study <- 100 * mean(method_days[[method$heatwave_main]])
method$stations_per_day <- range(method_days$o3_n_stations)

# The CR2MET municipal file: header (code, latitude, longitude, area) and series
method_header <- fread(input_path("cr2met_tmax"), header = FALSE, nrows = 4)
method_cr2met <- data.table(com = as.integer(unlist(method_header[1, -(1:3)])),
                            latitude = as.numeric(unlist(method_header[2, -(1:3)])),
                            area_km2 = as.numeric(unlist(method_header[4, -(1:3)])))
method$cr2met_municipalities <- nrow(method_cr2met)
# Number of cells of 0.01 degrees that make up each area: a cell measures
# 0.01 degrees of latitude (111.195 km per degree) by 0.01 degrees of longitude
method_cr2met[, cells := area_km2 / ((0.01 * 111.195)^2 * cos(latitude * pi / 180))]
method_cr2met <- merge(method$municipalities[, .(com = code, municipality = name)], method_cr2met, by = "com")
stopifnot(nrow(method_cr2met) == nrow(method$municipalities))
method$largest <- method_cr2met[which.max(area_km2)]
method$cells_departure <- max(abs(method_cr2met$cells - round(method_cr2met$cells)))

method_tmax <- read_cr2met(input_path("cr2met_tmax"), "tmax", method$municipalities$code)
method$cr2met_first <- min(method_tmax$date)
method$cr2met_last <- max(method_tmax$date)
method_tmax <- fill_calendar(method_tmax, "tmax", handling = get_param("temperature", "leap_day_handling"))
method_tmax[, warm := is_warm_season(date, get_param("study", "warm_season_months"))]
method_thresholds <- fread(file.path(dir_tables, "temperature_thresholds.csv"), encoding = "UTF-8")
method_tmax <- merge(method_tmax,
                     method_thresholds[season_rule == get_param("temperature", "percentile_season"), .(com, p95)],
                     by = "com")
method_reference <- method_tmax[year(date) >= method$reference_years[1] &
                                  year(date) <= method$reference_years[2] & !temp_filled]
# Share of the days of the reference period above the 95th percentile: of all
# the days, and of the warm-season days
method$share_hot_reference <- 100 * mean(method_reference$tmax > method_reference$p95)
method$share_hot_reference_warm <- 100 * method_reference[warm == TRUE, mean(tmax > p95)]
# The same share before the study years and in them, all the days of the year
method$share_hot_before <- 100 * method_reference[year(date) < method$years[1], mean(tmax > p95)]
method$share_hot_during <- 100 * method_reference[year(date) >= method$years[1] &
                                                    year(date) <= method$years[2], mean(tmax > p95)]
stopifnot(method$reference_years[1] < method$years[1], method$reference_years[2] >= method$years[2])

# The delivered air pollution file
method_delivered <- fread(input_path(paste0("sinca_", get_param("air_pollution", "series_version_main"))),
                          select = c("comuna", "date"))
method$delivered_rows <- nrow(method_delivered)
method$delivered_first <- min(as.Date(method_delivered$date))
method$delivered_last <- max(as.Date(method_delivered$date))
rm(method_delivered, method_exposure, method_tmax, method_reference)
```

*Scripts of this deliverable: `Code/10_exposure_temperature.R` to
`Code/18_exposure_time_series.R`. [Workflow and scripts](#sec-methods-workflow)
lists what each one reads and writes, and every section of the page names the
scripts and the files behind its tables and figures.*

## Aim and design {#sec-methods-aim}

The study asks whether heatwaves and high ozone, together, raise mortality
more than the sum of their separate effects. This deliverable builds and
checks the exposure side of that question: for every municipality and day, the
temperature, the heatwave indicators, the ozone concentration and the compound
exposure that combines them. The deaths and the models are the subject of the
next deliverables.

In the health analysis each death is compared with the other days of the same
municipality, year, month and day of the week (time-stratified case-crossover
design), with the exposure of the same day and of the
`r max(method$lags)` days before. The exposure therefore has to be right day
by day within each municipality, more than in its level between
municipalities: this is what the checks below look at first.

The work has four steps. Each is done by scripts that write their results to
files, and this page only reads and shows those files:

1. build the temperature, heatwave and air pollution variables of each
   municipality and day;
2. verify them: coverage, calendars, definitions, quality rules;
3. validate the ozone exposure against the measurements it comes from;
4. describe the exposures in space and time: maps and time series.

## Study area, period and unit of analysis {#sec-methods-study}

- **Area.** The `r nrow(method$municipalities)` municipalities of urban
  Santiago: the 32 of Santiago Province and Puente Alto. They are listed, with
  their official codes, in `config/municipalities.csv`.
- **Period.** The warm seasons of `r method$years[1]` to `r method$years[2]`:
  the days between 1 November and 31 March, that is January to March and
  November to December of each of those calendar years. They are
  `r fmt(method$days)` days.
- **Unit.** The municipality-day: `r fmt(method$municipality_days)` in the
  period of analysis. The exposure dataset holds every day of the study years
  and the `r method$lag_buffer` days before the first one
  (`r fmt(method$rows)` rows), because the health analysis needs the exposure
  of the days before each death.
- **Seasons and years.** Tables and figures by year use calendar years. The
  time series that follow a season use the warm season that starts in
  November, named by its two years: 2009/10 runs from 1 November 2009 to
  31 March 2010. The first and the last seasons of the period, 2008/09 and
  2020/21, are covered in part.

The files are kept exactly as received in `Data/Input`, which the scripts only
read. `Data/input_manifest.csv` lists each input file with its size and
checksum; every script checks the files it reads against that list and stops
if one is missing or is not the listed one, so that a result cannot come
unnoticed from another version of a file. `Data/README.md` describes each

Two public codes of the research team are the reference for the definitions;
they are not data:

  indicators;
- `pollution-interpolation-kriging-idw`, for the interpolation model and its
  parameters.

## Temperature {#sec-methods-temperature}

*Script: `Code/10_exposure_temperature.R`.*

CR2MET is a gridded product of daily precipitation and of daily maximum and
minimum temperature for continental Chile, on a regular grid of 0.05 degrees.
It is built with statistical models calibrated on quality-controlled station
records and fed with variables of the ERA5 reanalysis, topographic parameters
and land-surface temperature estimated from satellite (Boisier, 2023). The
project works with the series of that product by municipality.

**What a municipal value is.** The header of the municipal files gives, for
each municipality, its code, a latitude, a longitude and an area. For the 33
municipalities of the study every one of those areas is a whole number of
cells of 0.01 degrees, to within `r fmt(method$cells_departure, 2)` of a cell
(the areas are given to 0.1 km²): `r method$largest$municipality` has
`r fmt(round(method$largest$cells))` cells, `r fmt(method$largest$area_km2)` km².
This indicates that the municipal series were computed over a mask of the
whole territory of each municipality, drawn on a grid of 0.01 degrees. The
files do not say with which rule; this report takes each value as the mean
over the territory, which is how the values behave: the municipalities that
reach into the Andes are much colder than their urban area. The rule should be
confirmed with the team that produced the files
([Points to settle](#sec-points-to-settle)); its consequences are in
[Why the number of heatwave days differs between municipalities](#sec-heatwave-municipalities).

**Calendar.** The municipal files have no 29 February. Those days are filled
with the mean of 28 February and 1 March and marked in the column
`temp_filled`; they are left out of the percentile calculations
([CR2MET has no 29 February](#sec-leap-days)). Whether the calendar is aligned
with that of the air pollution data is checked separately
([Are the two calendars aligned?](#sec-calendar-alignment)).

## Heatwave definitions {#sec-methods-heatwaves}

*Script: `Code/10_exposure_temperature.R`; functions `consecutive_flag()` and
`excess_heat_factor()` of `Code/01_functions.R`.*

The analysis plan asks for the definitions of the reference code of the
research team (Blanco and others, 2026): three durations and five thresholds,
15 indicators in all. Each is a variable of the exposure dataset, equal to 1
on a heatwave day and to 0 on any other day.

**Thresholds.** For municipality $m$, the threshold $q_m$ is one of:

- the `r paste0(method$percentiles, "th", collapse = ", ")` percentile of its
  daily maximum temperature over
  `r paste(method$reference_years, collapse = " to ")`, computed over all the
  days of the year (`percentile_season: all_year`, as in the reference code)
  with the usual interpolation between order statistics (type 7);
- `r method$absolute_c` °C, the same for every municipality.

**Hot day.** Day $t$ is hot in municipality $m$ when its maximum temperature
is strictly above the threshold:

$$H_{m,t} = 1 \ \text{ if } \ T^{\max}_{m,t} > q_m, \qquad H_{m,t} = 0 \ \text{ otherwise.}$$

**Heatwave day.** Day $t$ is a heatwave day of duration $n$ when it is at
least the $n$-th consecutive hot day:

$$W^{(n)}_{m,t} = H_{m,t} \times H_{m,t-1} \times \dots \times H_{m,t-n+1}, \qquad n = 2, 3, 4.$$

The first $n - 1$ days of a hot spell are therefore not heatwave days: with
$n = 2$, a spell of five hot days has four heatwave days. Consecutive days are
counted within each municipality, on its complete calendar. The reference
script counts them over a table with all the municipalities stacked, which
gives other numbers
([Consecutive days must be counted within each municipality](#sec-consecutive-days)).

**Excess heat factor.** The fifth threshold is the excess heat factor (EHF)
of Nairn and Fawcett (2015), with the formulas of the reference code. Let
$D_{m,t} = \left(T^{\max}_{m,t} + T^{\min}_{m,t+1}\right) / 2$ be the daily
mean temperature (the variable `tad` of the dataset) and
$\bar{D}^{(k)}_{m,t}$ its mean over the $k$ days that end on day $t$. Then

$$\mathrm{EHI}^{\mathrm{sig}}_{m,t} = \bar{D}^{(n)}_{m,t} - D^{P`r method$ehf_percentile`}_{m}, \qquad
\mathrm{EHI}^{\mathrm{accl}}_{m,t} = \bar{D}^{(n)}_{m,t} - \bar{D}^{(`r method$ehf_days`)}_{m,t},$$

$$\mathrm{EHF}_{m,t} = \mathrm{EHI}^{\mathrm{sig}}_{m,t} \times \max\left(1, \ \mathrm{EHI}^{\mathrm{accl}}_{m,t}\right),$$

where $D^{P`r method$ehf_percentile`}_{m}$ is the
`r method$ehf_percentile`th percentile of the daily mean temperature of the
municipality over the reference period. A day is a heatwave day when
$\mathrm{EHF}_{m,t} > 0$, for $n = 2, 3, 4$. The original index uses a
three-day mean and compares it with the `r method$ehf_days` days before it;
here, as in the reference code, the same formulas are applied to the three
durations, and the two means end on the same day.

| Threshold | 2 days | 3 days | 4 days |
|:----------|:-----|:-----|:-----|
| 90th percentile of the municipality | `hw_p90_2d` | `hw_p90_3d` | `hw_p90_4d` |
| 95th percentile of the municipality | `hw_p95_2d` | `hw_p95_3d` | `hw_p95_4d` |
| 99th percentile of the municipality | `hw_p99_2d` | `hw_p99_3d` | `hw_p99_4d` |
| 30 °C | `hw_30c_2d` | `hw_30c_3d` | `hw_30c_4d` |
| Excess heat factor above zero | `hw_ehf_2d` | `hw_ehf_3d` | `hw_ehf_4d` |

: The 15 heatwave indicators of the exposure dataset, by threshold and minimum number of consecutive days. {#tbl-indicators}

**Working definition.** Where one definition has to be shown, the pages use
`r method$heatwave_main` (`r heatwave_label(method$heatwave_main)`). It is a
working value of `config/config.yml`, marked `TO CONFIRM`: the choice of the
headline definition belongs to the principal investigator, and the results are
given for the 15.

**What the percentile means in the warm season.** The percentile is taken
over all the days of the year, and the days above it are summer days. In the
reference period, `r fmt(method$share_hot_reference, 1)`% of all the days are
above the 95th percentile of their municipality, and
`r fmt(method$share_hot_reference_warm, 1)`% of the warm-season days. Those
days are not spread evenly over the period: they are
`r fmt(method$share_hot_before, 1)`% of the days of
`r method$reference_years[1]` to `r method$years[1] - 1` and
`r fmt(method$share_hot_during, 1)`% of the days of the study years. In the
warm seasons of `r method$years[1]` to `r method$years[2]`,
`r fmt(method$share_hot_study, 1)`% of the municipality-days are above the
threshold, and `r fmt(method$share_heatwave_study, 1)`% are heatwave days
under the working definition. A threshold from the warm-season days alone is
about one degree higher ([Temperature thresholds](#sec-thresholds)); which of
the two to use is one of the [points to settle](#sec-points-to-settle).

## Ozone and the other air pollution variables {#sec-methods-pollution}

The dataset holds three ozone series for each municipality and day, each by
two interpolation methods. All are in parts per billion (ppb).

::: {.wide-table}

| Series | Metric | Station values | Script |
|:---|:------|:------|:--------|
| `o3` | 24-hour mean | As prepared by the data author: trimmed and imputed | `Code/11_exposure_air_pollution.R` |
| `o3obs` | 24-hour mean | Rebuilt here from the validated hourly records | `Code/12_ozone_station_series.R` |
| `o3mda8` | Daily maximum 8-hour mean (MDA8), the metric named in the analysis plan | Rebuilt here from the validated hourly records | `Code/12_ozone_station_series.R` |

: Ozone series of the exposure dataset. Each has the suffix `_idw` or `_ok`, for the interpolation method. {#tbl-ozone-series}

:::

### The delivered series {#sec-methods-delivered}

*Script: `Code/11_exposure_air_pollution.R`.*

The delivered files hold one row per municipality and day
(`r fmt(method$delivered_rows)` rows). According to the description that came
with the delivery and to the repository of the model, the data author built
them in three steps:

1. **Station series.** Hourly SINCA records, trimmed at their 1st and 99th
   percentiles and averaged over the day when at least 12 hours are valid.
2. **Imputation.** The gaps of the daily station series are filled: PM2.5
   from PM10 by regression, the other variables with a random-forest method
   (`missForest`).
3. **Interpolation.** Each day is interpolated to one point per municipality,
   the municipal administration building, with the model described below.

There are two versions. Version `opr`, recommended by the data author and used
here, keeps the values of each monitor inside its period of operation; version
`all` also holds values modelled outside that period and is kept for
sensitivity analyses. From the delivered files this project takes ozone,
PM2.5, nitrogen dioxide and relative humidity; the last three are covariates
of the sensitivity analyses of deliverable 4. Units are as delivered: ppb for
ozone and nitrogen dioxide, µg/m³ for PM2.5, percent for humidity.

Two rules are applied to the delivered values, and their effect is counted in
[Ozone and co-pollutants: delivered series](#sec-delivered-series):

- a value built on fewer than `r get_param("air_pollution", "min_stations")`
  stations is set to missing;
- a value below zero, which ordinary kriging can produce, is set to missing.

### Ozone rebuilt from the hourly records {#sec-methods-rebuilt}

*Script: `Code/12_ozone_station_series.R`; functions `read_sinca_hourly()`,
`daily_from_hourly()` and `interpolate_day()` of `Code/01_functions.R`.*

The delivered ozone is a 24-hour mean computed after trimming and imputation,
and the analysis plan names the MDA8. Script 12 therefore rebuilds the station
series from the hourly records as SINCA publishes them, with no trimming and
no imputation:

- **Records used.** SINCA marks every hourly record as validated, preliminary
  or not validated. Only the records with status
  `r paste(unlist(method$station_rules$accepted_status), collapse = ", ")`
  are used.
- **24-hour mean** (`o3obs`). The mean of the hours of the day, when at least
  `r method$station_rules$min_valid_hours_day` are valid.
- **MDA8** (`o3mda8`). For each hour of the day, the mean of the 8 hours that
  end on it, when at least `r method$station_rules$mda8_min_hours_window` of
  the 8 are valid; the MDA8 is the highest of those running means, when at
  least `r method$station_rules$mda8_min_windows_day` of the 24 exist.
- **Stations.** The `r nrow(method$stations)` ozone stations of the
  Metropolitan Region:
  `r paste(method$stations$station, collapse = ", ")`.

The daily station values are then interpolated to the same target points with
the same model and parameters as the delivered series.

### The interpolation model {#sec-methods-interpolation}

*Function `interpolate_day()` of `Code/01_functions.R`, with the calls of the
data author's code; parameters under `interpolation` in `config/config.yml`.*

Stations and target points are in UTM zone 19 South
(EPSG `r method$interpolation$crs_epsg`), so that distances are in metres.
Each day is interpolated on its own, when at least
`r method$interpolation$ok_min_stations` stations have a value.

- **Inverse distance weighting (IDW).** The value at the target point $s_0$
  is the weighted mean of the stations, with weights that fall with the
  distance $d_i$ to each station:

  $$\hat{z}(s_0) = \frac{\sum_i w_i \, z(s_i)}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad w_i = d_i^{-`r method$interpolation$idw_power`},$$

  over at most the `r method$interpolation$idw_nmax` nearest stations within
  `r fmt(method$interpolation$idw_maxdist_m / 1000)` km. A point with no
  station within that distance has no value.
- **Ordinary kriging.** The variogram of the day is chosen and fitted
  automatically (`automap::autofitVariogram`), and each prediction comes with
  its variance. With very few stations a variogram cannot always be fitted:
  the day is then left without a kriging value, and counted.

IDW is the working method of the configuration. The two methods are compared
by cross-validation in [B. The interpolation model](#sec-validation-model).

### High ozone {#sec-methods-high-ozone}

*Script: `Code/13_exposure_merge_qc.R`; cut-offs in
`Output/Tables/ozone_cutoffs.csv`.*

A day has high ozone in a municipality when its value is above a percentile
of the values of that municipality over the warm-season days of the study
years. The percentiles are `r paste(method$cutoffs, collapse = ", ")`, for
each of the six series: `r length(method$ozone_flags)` flags, named like
`o3_idw_gt_p75`. The working definition is `r method$ozone_main` above the
`r method$cutoff_main`th percentile, also marked `TO CONFIRM`.

## Compound exposure {#sec-methods-compound}

*Script: `Code/13_exposure_merge_qc.R`; function `compound_category()` of
`Code/01_functions.R`.*

Each municipality-day falls in one of four categories, from a heatwave
indicator and a high-ozone flag:

::: {.no-download}

| Category | Heatwave | High ozone |
|:---|:---|:---|
| E00, neither | No | No |
| E10, heatwave only | Yes | No |
| E01, high ozone only | No | Yes |
| E11, heatwave and high ozone | Yes | Yes |

:::

A day without one of the two values is not classified. The frequencies are
tabulated for every combination of the `r length(method$heatwave_columns)`
heatwave indicators and the `r length(method$ozone_flags)` ozone flags
(`r length(method$heatwave_columns) * length(method$ozone_flags)` combinations),
by municipality and by year
([Across the grid of definitions](#sec-grid-definitions)).

## Quality control {#sec-methods-quality}

*Scripts: `Code/10_exposure_temperature.R` to `Code/13_exposure_merge_qc.R`.
A check that fails stops the script: no dataset is written with a known
defect.*

::: {.wide-table}

| Check | What is verified | Where |
|:-----|:--------------|:-------|
| Inputs | Every input file is the one listed in the manifest (size and checksum) | All the scripts |
| Coverage | Each source has exactly one row per municipality and day, for the same days, with no repeated and no missing rows | [Coverage of the three sources](#sec-coverage) |
| Calendar of the temperature | The only gaps are the 29 February days; any other gap stops the script | [CR2MET has no 29 February](#sec-leap-days) |
| Alignment of the calendars | Day-to-day changes of CR2MET temperature and of station temperature agree best with no shift, in leap years as in the others | [Are the two calendars aligned?](#sec-calendar-alignment) |
| Thresholds | Thresholds of each municipality under the two season rules | [Temperature thresholds](#sec-thresholds) |
| Heatwave indicators | The 15 indicators exist; consecutive days are counted within each municipality; comparison with the reference script; differences between municipalities | [Heatwave indicators](#sec-heatwave-indicators) |
| Delivered air pollution | Missing values, values below zero, values with too few stations; agreement of IDW and kriging; versions `opr` and `all` | [Ozone and co-pollutants: delivered series](#sec-delivered-series) |
| Rebuilt ozone | Validation status of the hourly records; days with too few stations; days with a variogram warning or without a fitted variogram | [Ozone rebuilt from the hourly records](#sec-rebuilt-series) |
| Dataset | One row per municipality and day; codebook with the missing values of every variable | [Exposure dataset, 2009-2020](#sec-exposure-dataset) |

: Quality control of the exposure data. {#tbl-quality}

:::

The functions behind the variables are also tested apart, on small examples
with a known answer (`tests/test_methods.R`), every time `Code/run_all.R`
runs.

## Validation of the ozone exposure {#sec-methods-validation}

*Scripts: `Code/12_ozone_station_series.R`, `Code/14_interpolation_validation.R`,
`Code/16_reanalysis_comparison.R` and `Code/17_validation_summary.R`.*

The ozone exposure is examined at the three points where it can go wrong
([Validation of the ozone exposure](#sec-ozone-validation)):

- **Station inputs.** The station series used by the data author are compared,
  station by station and day by day, with the 24-hour mean of the validated
  hourly records.
- **Interpolation model.** Leave-one-station-out cross-validation: for every
  warm-season day each station is removed in turn, the model is fitted to the
  others and the removed station is predicted. The agreement is measured by
  the bias, the mean absolute error, the root mean square error, the
  correlation and the coefficient of determination against the 1:1 line; for
  the classification of high-ozone days, by sensitivity, specificity and
  kappa.
- **Municipal series.** The delivered series is compared with the series
  rebuilt from the validated records with the same model, by level of ozone
  and on the classification of high-ozone days.

An independent source closes the validation: the CAMS reanalysis, which
assimilates satellite retrievals of ozone into a chemistry model (Inness and
others, 2019). Its cells are far larger than a municipality, so it is used
only for the day-to-day course of ozone over the city.

## Maps and time series {#sec-methods-series}

*Scripts: `Code/13_exposure_merge_qc.R` for the dataset and the frequency
tables; `Code/18_exposure_time_series.R` for the series of every
municipality.*

- **Maps.** One value per municipality over the days of analysis, drawn on the
  municipal polygons of the interpolation repository.
- **Series of every municipality.** Daily values, and their monthly and annual
  summaries: the mean of temperature and of ozone, and the number of heatwave
  days, of high-ozone days and of days with both.
- **Mean of the municipalities.** The plain mean of the 33 municipal values:
  every municipality counts the same, whatever its population or area. It
  describes the typical municipality, not the exposure of the population of
  the city.
- **Missing values.** Some municipality-days have no rebuilt ozone value.
  Means are taken over the days, or the municipalities, that have one, and the
  tables give their number.

then renders the pages. The scripts are not run when a page is rendered.

|:-------|:------|:--------------|:------|

| `Code/13_exposure_merge_qc.R` | The three datasets above | `Data/Derived/exposure_2009_2020.csv`; `Output/Tables/exposure_alignment.csv`, `temporal_alignment_lags.csv`, `ozone_cutoffs.csv`, `compound_frequency_by_municipality.csv`, `compound_frequency_by_year.csv`, `exposure_codebook.csv` | Coverage; calendars; exposure dataset; maps; compound exposure |

| `Code/16_reanalysis_comparison.R` | CAMS files; `interpolation_points.csv`; the exposure dataset | `Data/Derived/cams_ozone_daily.csv`, `cams_city_daily.csv`; `Output/Tables/validation_cams_cells.csv`, `validation_cams_correlation.csv` | Validation: the CAMS reanalysis |
| `Code/17_validation_summary.R` | `ozone_station_daily.csv`; the exposure dataset; the cross-validation predictions; the data author's station series | Nine tables `Output/Tables/validation_*.csv` | Validation, parts A, B and C |
| `Code/18_exposure_time_series.R` | The exposure dataset | `Output/Tables/series_daily_all_municipalities.csv`, `series_monthly_by_municipality.csv`, `series_annual_by_municipality.csv`; seven figures `Output/Figures/series_*`, each as PDF and as PNG at `r get_param("figures", "png_dpi")` dpi | Time series of every municipality |

: Scripts of this deliverable, with what each one reads and writes. {#tbl-workflow}

:::

Shared code: `Code/00_setup.R` (folders, configuration, checks of the inputs),
`Code/01_functions.R` (the functions named above) and `Code/02_plot_style.R`
(style of the figures and the function that writes figure files). All the
parameters are in `config/config.yml`; none is written in a script. The code
of every script is in [R scripts](#sec-scripts).

## Software and reproducibility {#sec-methods-software}

The analysis is written in R; the session information at the end of the page
gives the version of R and of the packages behind this rendering, and
`Output/run_environment.txt` those of the last complete run. The main
packages are `data.table` for the data, `sf` for the geometries, `gstat` and
`automap` for the interpolation, and `ggplot2` for the figures. The pages are
rendered with Quarto.

`Code/run_all.R` runs everything with one command: it checks the software and
the inputs, runs the tests of the methods and the scripts, renders the pages
and compares every table with its copy from before the run. The exposure
dataset is also rebuilt independently in Python and compared with the R
version column by column ([Exposure dataset in Python](py_01_exposure.html)).

## Limits of the exposure data {#sec-methods-limits}

- **Temperature is a value for the whole municipal territory, ozone a value
  at one point.** In the municipalities that reach into the Andes the
  temperature series describes the mountain more than the place where people
  live, while ozone is interpolated to the municipal building.
  `r method$largest$municipality` is the extreme case
  ([Why the number of heatwave days differs between municipalities](#sec-heatwave-municipalities)).
- **The percentile thresholds come from a period that contains the study
  years.** Days above the threshold are
  `r fmt(method$share_hot_during / method$share_hot_before, 1)` times as
  frequent in the study years as in the earlier years of the reference
  period, and most heatwave days fall in the last years of the study
  ([Time series of every municipality](#sec-series-municipalities)).
- **Few monitors.** Between `r method$stations_per_day[1]` and
  `r method$stations_per_day[2]` stations a day describe
  `r nrow(method$municipalities)` municipalities in the delivered series, and
  the eastern municipalities depend on one monitor
  ([What this means for the analysis](#sec-validation-conclusions)).
- **The delivered ozone is a 24-hour mean built on trimmed and imputed
  station series**, and it understates the days with most ozone. The plan
  names the MDA8. The three series are kept so that the choice can be made and
  its effect shown.
- **Ordinary kriging with a variogram fitted every day** is not reproducible
  to the last digit between machines, and its intervals are too narrow. IDW
  gives the same values on every machine.
- **Working definitions.** The heatwave definition, the ozone series, the
  ozone cut-off and the season of the percentiles are working values. The
  open choices are listed in [Points to settle](#sec-points-to-settle).

# Data verification and quality control {#sec-quality-control}

```{r}
#| label: setup-quality-control
#| include: false
source(here::here("Code", "00_setup.R"))
source(here::here("Code", "01_functions.R"))
source(here::here("Code", "02_plot_style.R"))
library(knitr)
theme_set(theme_report())
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")

read_table <- function(file) fread(file.path(dir_tables, file), encoding = "UTF-8")
exposure <- fread(derived_path("exposure_2009_2020.csv"), encoding = "UTF-8")
exposure[, date := as.Date(date)]
analysis <- exposure[in_study_period == TRUE & warm_season == TRUE]
n_mun <- uniqueN(analysis$com)
n_days <- uniqueN(analysis$date)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 0) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
```

## Purpose

This section verifies the exposure data of the study before any health analysis:
that temperature and air pollution cover the same municipalities and days, that
the heatwave indicators mean what the analysis plan says, and that the ozone
series are fit for use. The exposure dataset for 2009-2020 and the points that
need a decision follow in their own sections.

The unit is the municipality-day: `r n_mun` municipalities (Santiago Province
plus Puente Alto) and the `r fmt(n_days)` days between 1 November and 31 March
of the calendar years 2009 to 2020, that is `r fmt(nrow(analysis))`
municipality-days.

The sources of the data are described in
[Data sources](#sec-methods-sources) and the definitions in the rest of the
[Methodology](#sec-methodology). Every parameter used below is read from
`config/config.yml`.

## Coverage of the three sources {#sec-coverage}

*Script: `Code/13_exposure_merge_qc.R`. Table:
`Output/Tables/exposure_alignment.csv`.*

Each source must hold exactly one row per municipality and day, for the same
days. The dataset keeps the three days before 1 January 2009 so that deaths of
the first days have their lagged exposures.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-alignment
#| tbl-cap: "Coverage of each source on the municipality-by-day grid."
alignment <- read_table("exposure_alignment.csv")
kable(alignment, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Source", "Rows", "Municipalities", "First day", "Last day", "Days",
                    "Repeated rows", "Missing from grid", "Outside grid"))
```

The three sources cover the same `r fmt(alignment$rows[1])` municipality-days
with no repeated and no missing rows.

## Calendars

### CR2MET has no 29 February {#sec-leap-days}

*Computed in this page from the CR2MET file, with `read_cr2met()`. The days
are filled by `fill_calendar()` in `Code/10_exposure_temperature.R`.*

```{r}
#| label: leap-days
one <- read_cr2met(input_path("cr2met_tmax"), "tmax", study_municipalities()$code[1])
calendar <- seq(min(one$date), max(one$date), by = "day")
absent <- calendar[!calendar %in% one$date]
in_study <- absent[year(absent) >= 2009 & year(absent) <= 2020]
```

The CR2MET municipal files have `r fmt(nrow(one))` days between
`r format(min(one$date))` and `r format(max(one$date))`, against
`r fmt(length(calendar))` calendar days. The `r length(absent)` absent days are
all 29 February (`r paste(format(absent, "%Y"), collapse = ", ")`); three fall in
the study period (`r paste(format(in_study), collapse = ", ")`), which leaves
`r length(in_study) * n_mun` municipality-days without temperature.

The configuration sets `leap_day_handling` to
"`r get_param("temperature", "leap_day_handling")`": the pipeline fills those
days with the mean of 28 February and 1 March and marks them in `temp_filled`.
They are left out of the percentile calculations.

### Are the two calendars aligned? {#sec-calendar-alignment}

*Script: `Code/13_exposure_merge_qc.R`. Table:
`Output/Tables/temporal_alignment_lags.csv`.*

A file with 365 days per year could also be shifted by one day after each
29 February. The check below correlates the day-to-day change of the CR2MET
maximum temperature with the day-to-day change of the SINCA station
temperature, moved between two days earlier and two days later. Aligned
calendars give the highest correlation at a shift of zero, in leap years as in
the others.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lags
#| fig-cap: "Correlation between day-to-day changes of CR2MET maximum temperature and SINCA station temperature, by shift of the SINCA series."
#| fig-height: 3.4
lags <- read_table("temporal_alignment_lags.csv")
ggplot(lags, aes(factor(shift_days), correlation)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, fill = colour_method[["IDW"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", correlation), vjust = ifelse(correlation >= 0, -0.4, 1.3)),
            colour = ink$secondary, size = 3.2) +
  facet_wrap(~period) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.12, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "Shift of the SINCA series (days)", y = "Correlation")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lags
#| tbl-cap: "Values behind the figure."
kable(dcast(lags, period ~ shift_days, value.var = "correlation"), digits = 3)
```

The correlation peaks at a shift of zero in both periods: CR2MET dates are
calendar dates and the only difference is the missing 29 February.

## Temperature thresholds {#sec-thresholds}

*Script: `Code/10_exposure_temperature.R`. Table:
`Output/Tables/temperature_thresholds.csv`.*

Percentiles of the daily maximum temperature of each municipality over
`r paste(get_param("temperature", "percentile_reference_years"), collapse = "-")`.
The reference code computes them over all days of the year
(`percentile_season: all_year`, the value in use); the table also gives the
thresholds that the warm-season days alone would produce.

```{r}
#| label: fig-thresholds
#| fig-cap: "95th percentile of daily maximum temperature by municipality, reference period 1990-2020, under the two season rules."
#| fig-height: 6.2
thresholds <- read_table("temperature_thresholds.csv")
thresholds[, rule := fifelse(season_rule == "all_year", "All days of the year", "Warm-season days")]
order_mun <- thresholds[season_rule == "all_year"][order(p95), municipality]
ggplot(thresholds, aes(p95, factor(municipality, levels = order_mun), colour = rule)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = get_param("temperature", "absolute_threshold_celsius"),
             colour = ink$axis, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("All days of the year" = "#2a78d6", "Warm-season days" = "#eb6834")) +
  labs(x = "95th percentile of maximum temperature (°C)", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       caption = "Dashed line: the absolute threshold of 30 °C.")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Thresholds of maximum temperature by municipality (°C)."
wide <- dcast(thresholds, com + municipality ~ season_rule, value.var = c("p90", "p95", "p99"))
kable(wide[order(com)], digits = 1,
      col.names = c("Code", "Municipality", "P90 all year", "P90 warm", "P95 all year",
                    "P95 warm", "P99 all year", "P99 warm"))
```

The CR2MET municipal values describe the whole territory of the municipality
([Temperature](#sec-methods-temperature)). Municipalities that reach into the
Andes are therefore colder than their urban area: the 95th percentile ranges from
`r sprintf("%.1f", min(thresholds[season_rule == "all_year", p95]))` °C
(`r thresholds[season_rule == "all_year"][which.min(p95), municipality]`) to
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(thresholds[season_rule == "all_year", p95]))` °C
(`r thresholds[season_rule == "all_year"][which.max(p95), municipality]`). A
fixed threshold of 30 °C means very different things across municipalities,
while the percentile thresholds adapt to each one.

## Heatwave indicators {#sec-heatwave-indicators}

*Script: `Code/10_exposure_temperature.R` builds the indicators. The table and
the figure are computed in this page from the exposure dataset
(`Code/13_exposure_merge_qc.R`).*

A day is a heatwave day when it is at least the n-th consecutive day above the
threshold (n = 2, 3, 4), or when the excess heat factor of the last n days is
positive. The first n − 1 days of a hot spell are not flagged, as in the
reference code. The formulas are in
[Heatwave definitions](#sec-methods-heatwaves).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-heatwaves
#| tbl-cap: "Heatwave days in the warm seasons of 2009-2020 under the 15 definitions."
hw_columns <- grep("^hw_", names(analysis), value = TRUE)
hw_table <- rbindlist(lapply(hw_columns, function(v) {
  per_mun <- analysis[, .(days = sum(get(v))), by = com]
  data.table(indicator = v, municipality_days = sum(per_mun$days),
             share_pct = 100 * sum(per_mun$days) / nrow(analysis),
             per_municipality_year = mean(per_mun$days) / 12,
             min_municipality = min(per_mun$days), max_municipality = max(per_mun$days))
}))
kable(hw_table, digits = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0), format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Indicator", "Municipality-days", "% of days", "Days per municipality and year",
                    "Fewest in a municipality (12 years)", "Most in a municipality (12 years)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-heatwaves
#| fig-cap: "Heatwave days per municipality and year, by threshold and minimum duration."
#| fig-height: 3.6
hw_table[, threshold := factor(sub("^hw_(.*)_[0-9]d$", "\\1", indicator),
                               levels = c("p90", "p95", "p99", "30c", "ehf"),
                               labels = c("> P90", "> P95", "> P99", "> 30 °C", "EHF > 0"))]
hw_table[, duration := paste0(sub(".*_([0-9])d$", "\\1", indicator), " days")]
ggplot(hw_table, aes(duration, per_municipality_year)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, fill = ramp_orange[4]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", per_municipality_year)), vjust = -0.4,
            colour = ink$secondary, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~threshold, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "Minimum duration", y = "Days per municipality and year")
```

### Consecutive days must be counted within each municipality {#sec-consecutive-days}

*Computed in this page from the CR2MET file and the thresholds of
`Code/10_exposure_temperature.R`.*

The reference script (`HeatWave_PretermBirth_Chile`, `Code/2.0 HW_process_data.R`)
builds the indicators with `lag()` on a table that holds all municipalities
stacked and sorted by date. As published, the previous row of a municipality is
therefore another municipality on the same day, not the same municipality on the
previous day. The chunk below applies that logic and the within-municipality
logic to the same temperatures and thresholds.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reference-lag
#| tbl-cap: "Heatwave days (> P95) in the 33 municipalities, warm seasons 2009-2020: lag over stacked rows against lag within municipality."
# All municipalities of the Metropolitan Region, in the column order of the file
raw <- fread(input_path("cr2met_tmax"), header = FALSE)
file_codes <- as.integer(unlist(raw[1, -(1:3)]))
rm_codes <- file_codes[file_codes >= 13000 & file_codes < 14000]
stacked <- read_cr2met(input_path("cr2met_tmax"), "tmax", rm_codes)
stacked[, file_order := match(com, rm_codes)]
p95 <- thresholds[season_rule == get_param("temperature", "percentile_season"), .(com, p95)]
stacked <- merge(stacked, p95, by = "com", all.x = TRUE)
stacked[, hot := as.integer(tmax > p95)]

# As published: rows sorted by date, municipalities stacked, lag over rows
setorder(stacked, date, file_order)
for (n in 2:4) {
  stacked[, (paste0("rows_", n, "d")) := as.integer(Reduce(`+`, shift(hot, 0:(n - 1))) >= n)]
}
# Within municipality, over consecutive calendar rows of the file
setorder(stacked, com, date)
for (n in 2:4) {
  stacked[, (paste0("within_", n, "d")) := as.integer(Reduce(`+`, shift(hot, 0:(n - 1))) >= n),
          by = com]
}
compare <- stacked[com %in% study_municipalities()$code & year(date) %in% 2009:2020 &
                     month(date) %in% get_param("study", "warm_season_months")]
for (v in grep("^(rows|within)_", names(compare), value = TRUE)) {
  set(compare, which(is.na(compare[[v]])), v, 0L)
}
lag_compare <- rbindlist(lapply(2:4, function(n) {
  a <- compare[[paste0("rows_", n, "d")]]
  b <- compare[[paste0("within_", n, "d")]]
  data.table(duration = paste(n, "days"), hot_days = sum(compare$hot),
             stacked_rows = sum(a), within_municipality = sum(b),
             flagged_only_by_stacked = sum(a == 1 & b == 0),
             flagged_only_within = sum(a == 0 & b == 1))
}))
kable(lag_compare, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Minimum duration", "Days above P95", "Lag over stacked rows",
                    "Lag within municipality", "Flagged only by stacked rows",
                    "Flagged only within municipality"))
```

With the stacked-row lag, a single hot day is flagged as a heatwave whenever the
neighbouring municipalities in the file are also hot that day, so the number of
heatwave days barely falls as the required duration grows. Counting within each
municipality gives the indicators used in this project. The published indicators
of the reference repository should be checked against this before they are
reused.

### Why the number of heatwave days differs between municipalities {#sec-heatwave-municipalities}

*Computed in this page from the exposure dataset
(`Code/13_exposure_merge_qc.R`), the thresholds of
`Code/10_exposure_temperature.R`, the header of the CR2MET file and the target
points of the interpolation. The indicator is computed again here with
`consecutive_flag()` and has to equal the one of the dataset.*

The threshold is a percentile of each municipality, so the number of days
above it is nearly the same everywhere. The number of heatwave days is not.
The table takes the indicators of the 95th percentile apart, municipality by
municipality.

```{r}
#| label: heatwave-municipalities
main_rule <- get_param("temperature", "percentile_season")
other_rule <- setdiff(c("all_year", "warm_season"), main_rule)
rule_label <- c(all_year = "all the days of the year", warm_season = "the warm-season days")

# Hot spells: runs of consecutive days above the threshold, on the complete
# calendar of each municipality
calendar <- exposure[order(com, date), .(com, municipality, date, in_study_period, warm_season,
                                         tmax, hot_p95, hw_p95_2d, hw_p95_3d, hw_p95_4d)]
stopifnot(calendar[, all(diff(date) == 1), by = com]$V1)
calendar[, spell := rleid(hot_p95), by = com]
calendar[, change := tmax - shift(tmax), by = com]
# The indicator of the dataset is what the definition says
calendar[, check_2d := consecutive_flag(hot_p95, 2), by = com]
stopifnot(calendar[!is.na(check_2d), all(check_2d == hw_p95_2d)])
# The same count with the thresholds of the other season rule
calendar <- merge(calendar, thresholds[season_rule == other_rule, .(com, p95_other = p95)], by = "com")
setorder(calendar, com, date)
calendar[, hw_other_2d := consecutive_flag(as.integer(tmax > p95_other), 2), by = com]
season_days <- calendar[in_study_period == TRUE & warm_season == TRUE]
spells <- season_days[hot_p95 == 1, .(days = .N, first = min(date), last = max(date)),
                      by = .(com, spell)]

# Territory behind the temperature series, and distance from its centre to the
# point where ozone is interpolated. The header of the CR2MET file gives the
# code, the latitude, the longitude (to 0.01 degrees, about 1 km) and the area
# of each municipality.
cr2met_header <- fread(input_path("cr2met_tmax"), header = FALSE, nrows = 4)
territory <- data.table(com = as.integer(unlist(cr2met_header[1, -(1:3)])),
                        latitude = as.numeric(unlist(cr2met_header[2, -(1:3)])),
                        longitude = as.numeric(unlist(cr2met_header[3, -(1:3)])),
                        area_km2 = as.numeric(unlist(cr2met_header[4, -(1:3)])))
territory <- merge(study_municipalities()[, .(com = code, municipality = name)], territory, by = "com")
ozone_points <- new.env()
load(input_path("interpolation_locations"), envir = ozone_points)
ozone_points <- ozone_points$interpol
stopifnot(setequal(ozone_points$comuna, territory$municipality))
centres <- sf::st_transform(sf::st_as_sf(territory, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326),
                            sf::st_crs(ozone_points))
territory[, distance_km := as.numeric(sf::st_distance(
  centres, ozone_points[match(municipality, ozone_points$comuna), ], by_element = TRUE)) / 1000]

by_municipality <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "com"), list(
  season_days[, .(tmax = mean(tmax), hot_days = sum(hot_p95), hw_2d = sum(hw_p95_2d),
                  hw_3d = sum(hw_p95_3d), hw_4d = sum(hw_p95_4d), hw_other_2d = sum(hw_other_2d),
                  sd_change = sd(change)), by = .(com, municipality)],
  spells[, .(spells = .N, mean_length = mean(days), longest = max(days)), by = com],
  thresholds[season_rule == main_rule, .(com, p95)],
  territory[, .(com, area_km2, distance_km)]))
stopifnot(nrow(by_municipality) == n_mun, !anyNA(by_municipality))
setorder(by_municipality, -hw_2d)
most <- by_municipality[1]
fewest <- by_municipality[.N]
longest_spell <- spells[com == most$com][which.max(days)]
others <- by_municipality[com != most$com]
# Series more than 2 °C colder than the median municipality
colder <- by_municipality[com != most$com & tmax < median(tmax) - 2][order(tmax), municipality]
# Quoted in "Points to settle", at the end of the page
andes_point <- sprintf(
  "In %s it is %s °C colder than in the median municipality and gives the most heatwave days of the 33: %d, against %d to %d in the others",
  most$municipality, fmt(median(by_municipality$tmax) - most$tmax, 1), most$hw_2d,
  min(others$hw_2d), max(others$hw_2d))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-heatwave-municipalities
#| tbl-cap: "Days above the 95th percentile and heatwave days by municipality, warm seasons 2009-2020, with the territory behind each temperature series. Municipalities in order of heatwave days."
kableExtra::scroll_box(
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    kable(by_municipality[, .(municipality, area_km2, distance_km, tmax, p95, hot_days, spells,
                              mean_length, longest, hw_2d, hw_3d, hw_4d, hw_other_2d, sd_change)],
          format = "html", digits = c(0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2),
          format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
          col.names = c("Municipality", "Territory of the temperature series (km²)",
                        "From its centre to the ozone point (km)", "Mean maximum temperature (°C)",
                        "95th percentile (°C)", "Days above the 95th percentile", "Hot spells",
                        "Mean length of the spells (days)", "Longest spell (days)",
                        "Heatwave days, 2 days or more", "3 days or more", "4 days or more",
                        paste("2 days or more, threshold from", rule_label[[other_rule]]),
                        "SD of the day-to-day change of temperature (°C)")),
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), font_size = 12),
  height = "420px"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-heatwave-municipalities
#| fig-cap: "Heatwave days of each municipality against the mean length of its hot spells, warm seasons 2009-2020. One point per municipality."
#| fig-height: 3.8
labelled <- by_municipality[com %in% c(most$com, fewest$com)]
ggplot(by_municipality, aes(mean_length, hw_2d)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 2.8, fill = ramp_orange[4], colour = ink$surface, stroke = 0.6) +
  geom_text(data = labelled, aes(label = municipality), colour = ink$secondary, size = 3.2,
            hjust = ifelse(labelled$com == most$com, 1.15, -0.15)) +
  labs(x = "Mean length of the hot spells (days)",
       y = sprintf("Heatwave days (%s)", heatwave_label("hw_p95_2d")))
```

- **The days above the threshold are almost the same.** Between
  `r min(by_municipality$hot_days)` and `r max(by_municipality$hot_days)` of
  the `r fmt(n_days)` days of analysis, in every municipality.
- **Their grouping is not.** A spell of five hot days has four heatwave days
  under the two-day definition, and five single hot days have none: hot days
  that come in fewer and longer spells give more heatwave days.
  `r most$municipality` has `r most$hot_days` hot days in `r most$spells`
  spells, `r fmt(most$mean_length, 2)` days long on average; the longest
  lasted `r longest_spell$days` days, from `r format(longest_spell$first)` to
  `r format(longest_spell$last)`. `r fewest$municipality` has
  `r fewest$hot_days` hot days in `r fewest$spells` spells of
  `r fmt(fewest$mean_length, 2)` days, none longer than `r fewest$longest` days.
  Across the 33 municipalities, the heatwave days and the mean length of the
  spells have a correlation of `r fmt(cor(by_municipality$hw_2d, by_municipality$mean_length), 2)`.
- **The difference grows with the duration.** With two days or more:
  `r most$hw_2d` heatwave days in `r most$municipality` against
  `r fewest$hw_2d` in `r fewest$municipality`; with four or more:
  `r most$hw_4d` against `r fewest$hw_4d`.
- **It does not come from the season of the percentile.** With the threshold
  from `r rule_label[[other_rule]]` the heatwave days are between
  `r min(by_municipality$hw_other_2d)` and `r max(by_municipality$hw_other_2d)`,
  and `r by_municipality[which.max(hw_other_2d), municipality]` still has the
  most.

**Why `r most$municipality`.** Its series is the coldest by far (mean maximum
`r fmt(most$tmax, 1)` °C, against `r fmt(min(others$tmax), 1)` to
`r fmt(max(others$tmax), 1)` °C in the others) and the one that changes least
from one day to the next: the standard deviation of the day-to-day change is
`r fmt(most$sd_change, 2)` °C, against `r fmt(min(others$sd_change), 2)` to
`r fmt(max(others$sd_change), 2)` °C. A hot day is therefore followed more
often by another hot day. The series describes a territory of
`r fmt(most$area_km2)` km², `r fmt(most$area_km2 / max(others$area_km2), 0)`
times the next largest, and the point where the ozone of the municipality is
interpolated is `r fmt(most$distance_km, 1)` km from the centre of that
territory (the median of the 33 municipalities is
`r fmt(median(by_municipality$distance_km), 1)` km). The reading that follows
is an interpretation, not a result: a value for a large mountain territory
follows the slow changes of the air mass, and misses the day-to-day changes
of the valley floor, where the people of the municipality live.

**What it means for the analysis.** Within a municipality the indicator is
consistent: it marks the days that are hot for that series, and the health
analysis compares days of the same municipality. What is not assured is that
a heatwave day of the series is a heatwave day where people live. This
concerns `r most$municipality` above all, and to a smaller degree the other
series that are more than 2 °C colder than the median municipality
(`r paste(colder, collapse = ", ")`). The options are in
[Points to settle](#sec-points-to-settle).

#| label: tbl-pollution-summary

  data.table(variable = variables[[v]], idw_mean = mean(idw, na.rm = TRUE),

}))

### Version `opr` against version `all`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-versions
#| tbl-cap: "Ozone in the two delivered versions, warm seasons 2009-2020."
all_version <- fread(derived_path("exposure_air_pollution_all.csv"), encoding = "UTF-8",
                     select = c("com", "date", "o3_idw", "o3_ok", "o3_n_stations"))
all_version[, date := as.Date(date)]
versions <- merge(analysis[, .(com, date, o3_idw, o3_ok, o3_n_stations)], all_version,
                  by = c("com", "date"), suffixes = c("_opr", "_all"))
version_table <- rbindlist(lapply(c("idw", "ok"), function(m) {
  a <- versions[[paste0("o3_", m, "_opr")]]
  b <- versions[[paste0("o3_", m, "_all")]]
  data.table(method = m, municipality_days = sum(!is.na(a) & !is.na(b)),
             identical_pct = 100 * mean(abs(a - b) < 1e-6, na.rm = TRUE),
             correlation = cor(a, b, use = "complete.obs"),
             mean_difference = mean(b - a, na.rm = TRUE),
             p95_abs_difference = quantile(abs(b - a), 0.95, na.rm = TRUE))
}))
kable(version_table, digits = c(0, 0, 1, 3, 2, 2), format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Method", "Municipality-days", "Identical (%)", "Correlation",
                    "Mean difference, all − opr (ppb)", "95th percentile of absolute difference (ppb)"))
```
